translation:
That is why Kripanath had to go there — for the Word itself is God.

Now the question of who Kripanath is need not detain us here, for the two preceding chapters have already discussed this at length. This chapter opens with these very words. Looking at them, a question arises: where did Kripanath have to go, and why did he have to go? We have earlier called Kripanath one who loves His devotees (bhakta-vatsal). Such a devotee-loving Parbrahm must go to many places, because although He is free of all bondage, He allows Himself to be bound by His own devotees. He commands the five elements and the three gunas and yet is free of them; He acts, yet remains untouched by action; nothing at all touches Him; He has no birth, no old age, no death, no decay — imperishable (akshay), beyond the senses (agochar) is this Parbrahm, whom Jaidevji has sung of, whom Adhyaruji has sung of. But such a devotee-devoted Parbrahm — who can make Him known? We have already spoken of His form (swarup); it is only through that form that He can be recognised. Just as a traveller on an unfamiliar road repeatedly asks his way of a guide, and, led and inspired by such a guide, advances toward his true destination, so too does the one advancing on the path of spiritual devotion move forward with the support of the Sadguru, who is his guide. Only with the strength and support of the Guru — the Sadguru — can Parbrahm be known. On the soil of India the saints and great souls have shown the immense glory of the Guru-disciple bond. Devotees such as Kabir, Mira, and Narsinh, among others, have likewise described this Guru-disciple relationship at length. Since that subject is to be taken up in later chapters, it is not discussed further here.

But here, at the very outset, the question was raised: what does it mean that God "had to go"? If we answer it, this is simply Parbrahm's own natural, fundamental disposition — that is, His quality (lakshan). He pervades everywhere, and although present everywhere at once, He remains, in a special sense, closer to His devotees. Again the question arises: if He is near, then in what way is He near? He is not visible. What, then, is He? And if He is far, then how far is He? We answer: Parbrahm cannot be seen through the medium of the body and the like, for He does not become perceptible through the body or any other such component medium. Nor is He, like every embodied soul, bound up in worldly cause and action; and yet He appears bound by the condition of embodiment (upadhi), in the same way that the world is bound by the discriminating intellect (bheda-buddhi). And through the use of words, that very same single reality is separated out and seen as many different things by this discriminating intellect. Take an example: in a pot, a water-vessel (kamandal), a tunnel, and the like, there is space — that is, a hollow — present within each. Yet ordinary embodied souls commonly call it ghatakash, that is, "the space (the hollow, the air) contained within the pot." In just this way, differences regarding God have arisen even within such relations. The Shwetashvatara Upanishad says—

_Na tasya karyam karanam cha vidyate, na tatsamashchabhyadhikashcha drashyate |_
_Parasya shaktirvividhaiva shruyate, swabhaviki gyanabalakriya cha ||1||_
(Shweta-3-11)

(He, the Ishwar, has no action, that is, no body, and no instrument, that is, no organ of sense; nor is there anyone equal to Him or greater than Him. But His supreme power is heard of through His manifold and varied works, and His activity is known through the power of knowledge, that is, His inherent understanding.)

_Apanipado javano grahita, pashyatyachakshuh sa shrunotyakarnah |_
_Sa vetti vedyam na cha tasyaasti vetta, tamahuragryam purusham mahantam ||2||_
(Shweta-3-11)

(Though without hands or feet, He grasps and holds, and He moves with swiftness; though without eyes He sees, though without ears He hears. He knows all that is to be known, yet none can know Him as He is known — and for this they call Him the foremost, the great, primordial Being.)

That is why we say: the Word itself is the Supreme — for it is only through the Guru's words that He can be known, that He can be recognised. The words spoken of here are the words of Kabirji, of Gopaldasji, and of Jivanji Maharaj. Thus the devotees who have become gurumukh (turned toward the Guru) should listen to the Guru's words with faith, and should receive them. They should not view them with a worldly eye, but with the eye of ultimate truth (paramarthik drishti) — for when seen with a worldly eye, discriminating intellect (bheda-buddhi) arises and truth cannot be understood. This same matter, pointed to earlier in the scriptures, Adhyaruji has expounded in plain and simple Gujarati, in the words of his kadvu (devotional canto).

_Chidanandam parabrahma dhyanagamyam sanatanam |_
_Aksharam nirmalam nityam nirakaram namamyaham ||3||_

(I bow to that Parbrahm, of the very nature of consciousness and bliss, attainable through meditation — the eternal, imperishable, stainless, everlasting, formless Parbrahm.)

_Sur muni antariksh stave re gokul, hari te ati re akal |_
_Hari hari rame re govind, anand bharyo e ||1||_
_Aapanape ramato pindara ramade, hari te rame ne ramade |_
_Harite jame ne jamade, harino gagan brahmadik vichar kare e ||2||_
_Akal ramat mandi gokul mahen, ramat brahmadik chahe |_
_Hari te aapanape ade na abhade e ||3||_

(The sage-gods dwelling in the heavens sing this hymn of praise about Gokul — how utterly inconceivable Hari is! Hari, Hari — Govind sports, ever filled with bliss. Sporting in His own being, He makes the embodied souls sport with Him too; He Himself plays and makes others play, He Himself feeds and makes others feed; even Brahma and the other gods can only wonder at Hari's vast, sky-like being. Having set this ungraspable play in motion within Gokul, Brahma and the other gods long to share in it — yet Hari, sporting in His own being, is never sullied or touched by any of it.)

The sage-gods who dwell in the heavens sing the praises of such a Being — one so inconceivable that none can grasp or recognise Him — that blissful Govind who is enacting all this "play," this "lila." And He draws us too into it. His play, His lila, has no end or limit; even Brahma and the other gods behold it with wonder and astonishment.

That is, one who has become gurumukh should reflect upon such words with patient endurance (titiksha). This play of Parbrahm the original world-teacher Shankaracharya has called "maya." Vallabhacharya has called it "lila." Adhyaruji calls it Parbrahm's "ramat" (sport, play). For as soon as the word "maya" is used, a discriminating intellect readily arises between the soul (atma) and the Supreme Soul (paramatma). Once such a distinction arises, the individual soul (jivatma) becomes separated. In truth the jivatma is bound, without distinction, to every one of Parbrahm's works, and is a co-participant in them. Further, in the term "lila," used by the earlier school (purvapaksha), the jivatma is set apart from Parbrahm, and the jivatma's place in Parbrahm's works becomes secondary. Parbrahm alone pervades everywhere and thereby creates the distinction. Moreover, in this the identity (tadatmya) of atma and paramatma comes to be forgotten, for Parbrahm alone becomes the principal doer, and once such supremacy is asserted, the identity is destroyed.

Here a doubt arises: on the path of worship, where exactly do words such as "maya" and "lila" become an obstruction? The answer may be given thus: those who surrender everything as "Krishnarpan" (an offering to Krishna) and live their whole lives in pure, desireless devotion have no need to know anything further or to perform any special action, for one who offers everything to Parbrahm and lives merely to sustain the body has, for himself, no place left at all for "the world" — and for him words like "maya" and "lila" become useless. And yet, what of those who have not yet become wholly absorbed and merged in Parbrahm, or those seeking devotees still eager to know more of dharma? For them, more must be said. Unlettered women devotees such as Harmaba, Kunvarbai, and Panabai placed complete faith and trust in the Guru's words and offered everything as Krishnarpan, and so crossed the ocean of worldly existence with ease. But for knowledgeable and inquiring seekers such as Gopaldas and Krishnadas, it must be explained at length. If we look here according to the Vedantic view, first comes Shankaracharya. His doctrine is: Brahm satya, jagat mithya, jivo brahmaivanaparah — that is, Brahm-Ishwar is true (satya), and the world — that is, maya — is false (mithya); the individual soul (jiva) is Brahm itself and nothing else. But then the question arises: if everything whatsoever is Brahm and nothing else exists, then why should "maya" be called false? Why should it stand apart from Brahm? Here this discriminating thought arises: if the jivatma itself is Brahm, then why could maya too not be called a form of that very Brahm? For this reason this doctrine cannot be established as fully complete.

Vallabhacharya, on the other hand, in place of the word "maya," used the word "lila," and further stated his own doctrine thus—

_Sarve khalvidam brahma neha nanaasti kinchana |_
_Brahma satyam, jaganmithya jivo brahmaivanaparah ||4||_

(All this indeed is Brahm; here there is no plurality whatsoever. Brahm is true, the world is not false, the jiva is Brahm itself and nothing else.)

Brahm is true, the world is not false, the jiva is Brahm itself — in this way he attempted to show a unity. Yet in order to make clear the relation between jiva, world, and Brahm, he too had to say that all this is merely Parbrahm's "lila." And for self-liberation, for "moksha," Brahm's grace (kripa) is needed; without His grace the jivatma cannot be uplifted — that is, cannot attain the movement toward liberation.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has given no sanction at all to words such as "lila," "moksha," "mukti," and has not thought it right to cast the world into the snare of such words. We, he says, are simply His creatures; we live with Him, we eat with Him, we sleep with Him, and thus, going about our worldly work, we remain just as He keeps us — for Shri Krishna says in the Bhagavad Gita—

_Yad yad vibhutimat sattvam shrimad urjitam eva va |_
_Tat tad evavagaccha tvam mama tejo'nshasambhavam ||5||_
(Gita 10-41)

(Whatever being is possessed of glory, of splendour, or of vigour, know all of that to have sprung from a mere spark of My own radiance.)

Shri Krishna tells Arjuna: whatever being (jivatma) is endowed with lordly power, adorned with grace and fortune, or filled with vigorous, radiant strength — know all of them to be born from a mere fragment of My splendour; or know that it is by that very splendour that the world stands firm.

Thus, whatever disposition (bhava) a person sees Him with, in that same disposition he attains Him. Further, in this world some worship Him desiring heaven; some worship Him to gain release from the cycle of birth and death; some remember Him only to increase the fruits of their action (karma); and yet others worship Him with no expectation whatsoever.

_Antakale cha mameva smaran muktva kalevaram |_
_Yah prayati sa madbhavam yati nastyatra samshayah ||6||_
(Gita 8-5)

(Whatever soul departs at the time of death remembering Me alone, giving up the body, attains My very being — of this there is no doubt.)

The jivatma who, at the time of death, departs remembering none but Me, attains Me — of this, harbour no doubt.

_Yam yam vaapi smaran bhaavam tyajatyante kalevaram |_
_Tam tam eva iti kaunteya sada tadbhaavabhaavitah ||7||_
(Gita 8-6)

(O Kaunteya! Whatever state a man remembers when he finally quits the body, to that very state he goes, ever having been shaped by that same disposition.)

O Kaunteya! Whatever thing a person remembers as he leaves the body at the end, in that very disposition does the jivatma attain that thing.

The purport is this: as one's inner longing (vasana) has been, so is one's destiny. Thus those who become gurumukh and surrender everything to Him attain a good destiny — and this is why we say: the Word itself is the Supreme. That is, the Guru's word should be accepted with faith, and it is only in this way that Parbrahm can be attained — of this, hold no doubt or suspicion whatsoever.

Having looked at this preliminary groundwork, let us now come to our actual subject: what do the words of our Sadguru say?

That is why Kripanath had to go there, because of Ambarish's devotion to Ram, for his protection — for the Word itself is God — and Baba Kabirji bears witness to this. That is, God comes to fulfil His devotees' heartfelt wishes: trusting in such words of the Guru, Ambarish worshipped Him, and so the Lord had to come there. Thus the saying that the Word itself is the Supreme has proved true. That very Ishwar danced together with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu; He came swiftly at the sound of Narsinh's cymbals; and He became absorbed too in Mira's love. So what does Baba Kabir say?

_Ladha hai kachhu ladha hai hira, kamariye bandha hai ||1||_
_Avaran ek akal avinashi, ghatghat vyapi raha harate ||2||_
_Aho jhaako mool na tol map, kachhu nahi ganate gaan na hoi re |_
_Na kachhu halka na kachhu bhari, paar lakhe na koi re ||3||_
_Jaame ham soi ham maanhe, jal tarang jem ek bhaya |_
_Em jhaanat nar koi na marasi, van jaane nar bohot moova ||4||_
_Kahet kabir ram ras paaya, peevanhaar na paau re |_
_Bidhike vachan pahechaanat naahi, to kaadhi kaahaa dekhlaau re nar ||5||_

(Kabirji says: I have found something, I have found a diamond, and I have bound it tight to my waist. Formless, indescribable, unfathomable, imperishable, that Hari pervades every single vessel of being. Ah, He has no root, no weight, no measure — nothing about Him can be counted or sung. He is neither light nor heavy; none can fathom His limit. In Him I dwell, and I dwell in Him — we have become one, as a wave becomes one with water. Whoever truly knows this will never die; those who do not know it, many indeed have died. Kabir declares: I have obtained the taste of Ram's nectar, yet I find none to drink of it with me. Those who do not recognise the Creator's word — what, then, can I bring out and show them?)

That is: Kabirji tells us — "I have found something, I have found something as priceless as a diamond" — the word "Ram," obtained through the Guru, which he has taken firm hold of. It is beyond all reckoning of worth. So that this diamond, in the form of Hari, might never be lost or forgotten, he has bound it tight — that is, cinched it firmly — into his own inner being. That diamond is formless, beyond the measure of place or time, ungraspable by anyone, imperishable, and pervades every single vessel of existence. It has no weight, no measure; those who attempt to measure it possess no true knowledge — they are the ignorant, for the Supreme is beyond all measure. The Supreme is neither light nor heavy, nor can it be called this or that by anyone; none can reach its limit. He is in me, and I am in Him — the Supreme is the water of Brahm, and I am its ripple; that is, the soul and the Supreme Soul are one. Such is the name of "Ram" that has come to Kabirji. Thus the word obtained through the Guru is itself the word denoting Parbrahm; one should therefore place faith in such words and follow them. Here a doubt arises: why "Ram" alone — is there no other word? The word "Ram" is not the name of any particular individual but is the word denoting Parbrahm; it has not been applied here to signify any specific person, for this is the Sadguru's word. Then the question arises: what is the guarantee of that? Continuing, Kabirji explains that whoever truly knows this will never die — that is, those who have known the Supreme in His true essence have crossed the ocean of worldly existence and are freed from birth and death; those who do not know Him, many indeed have perished in ignorance. Baba Kabir says: I have obtained the taste of Ram's nectar, and I drink of it, and I long to give it to others too — but I find none willing to drink. So to whom shall I offer this Ram-rasa? And even when I offer it, they do not drink. The Creator's word — the utterance of Brahm, the eternal, ultimate truth — I explain as the name of Ram, yet they do not understand that word; what, then, can I bring out and show them — how, like Hanuman, could I tear open my own chest to show it?

In this pad, in Granth No. 8, page 21, a third verse appears as an addition, as follows:

_Puran brahm sakalmein ekai, ghat ghat bhitar aap rahai |_
_Bahar bhitar sakal nirantar, taaso dooja kaun kahe ||6||_

(The complete Brahm is one and the same in all; He Himself dwells within every single vessel of being. Outside and within, He remains constantly, unbrokenly one throughout; how, then, could anyone call another separate from Him?)

Meaning: the complete Brahm is one and the same, the very same, in every single being. Within every single body He Himself resides. Outside or within, He is present in the same unbroken way in everything; hence how can He be said to be anything separate from ourselves?

The names given to God, that is, His words, are indeed many, while God is one — so which of these words should be heeded? Hear now the source from which all these words arise — a sakhi:

_Sarkho saakshi sarvamein, jyun bhaajanmein bhaan |_
_Brahma keet patangalu, kahe kubera praan ||1||_

(The witness within every being is alike, as the sun is reflected alike in every vessel of water; whether in Brahma, in an insect, in a moth, or even, so to speak, in Kubera, the life-breath within is one and the same.)

Meaning: just as the sun appears the same in every vessel filled with water, so the Supreme is alike, one and the same, in every embodied being. Whether in Brahma or in an insect or a moth or even in Kubera, the life-breath — the jiva — is likewise one and the same.

_Sikhi saakhi laakh mile, kirtaniya paanch karod |_
_Koi brahm chine chinaave, te aage rahu kar jod ||2||_

(Those who have merely memorised sayings by rote number in the lakhs, and hired singers of kirtan number in the crores; but should I find even one who truly knows Brahm and can help others know Him, before that one I would stand with folded hands.)

Meaning: those who, like parrots, have simply memorised sayings and couplets about devotion to God — such people can be found in the lakhs; and those who sing kirtan for a fee, out of self-interest, may number as many as five crores. But should one find even a single person who truly and rightly knows God and could grant a true realisation of Him, one should submit oneself to him and, with folded hands, take refuge at his feet.

_Paanch pahar dhandha kiya, teen pahar rahya soy |_
_Ek pahar hari na bhajya, to mukti kaanse hoy ||3||_

(Five watches of the day were spent in worldly toil, three watches of the night in sleep; not even a single watch was given to remembering Hari — so from where, then, could liberation come?)

Meaning: five pahors (watches) were spent in household work, employment, and business; three pahors of the night were spent asleep; but not even a single pahor was given to the remembrance of God — so how, then, could liberation be attained?

_Kabir ja karan jag dhundhata, so to ghatahi maanhi |_
_Padda diya bharamka, taathe soojhat naahi ||4||_

(Kabir says: that which he was searching for throughout the world was, all along, within his own being; but a veil of delusion had been drawn over it, and so it could not be seen.)

Meaning: he who was searching throughout the world for God was, all the while, present within his own being — but a veil of illusion (bharam) had been cast over it, and so he could not see Him.

_Arab kharab vaani kathi, granth koti hazaar |_
_Karta purush kabir hai, naabhe kiyo vichaar ||5||_

(Utterances beyond count, arbs and kharabs, have been spoken, and thousands upon thousands, crores, of scriptures composed; yet Nabha, upon reflection, concluded that Kabir alone is the Creator-Person.)

Meaning: Nabha Swami, in composing the Bhaktamal, spoke words beyond counting — arbs and kharabs — and even composed thousands and crores of scriptures; yet Nabhaji became certain that it is Kabirji alone who is the form of the Creator, the Supreme Person, the Parmatma Himself. All other utterances pertain merely to the characters and deeds of His devotees.

Kabirji is eager to have all drink the nectar of divine love, and those who have drunk of this nectar he has briefly described in the Bijak, Shabda 12. In Kabirvani, issue 21, page 2, he has also discussed this at length, where it is stated: "Here a doubt arises — have there truly ever been such saints as have drunk the cup of the nectar of loving devotion?" Sadguru Kabirji answers this by saying that Gorakhnath, Dattatreya, Vashishtha, Vyas, Hanuman, Narad, and Shukdev Muni, and others, gathered together and sat in an assembly together with Shambhu and the Sanakadik sages — and upon the lips of every one of them rests the cup of the nectar of loving devotion. Ambarish, Yagyavalkya, King Janak, and Jad Bharat have drunk of this nectar of love, and Sheshnag has tasted this nectar of love through his thousand mouths — the count cannot be exhausted. In this way the devotees Dhruv, Prahlad, and Vibhishan too became intoxicated with love. Parvatiji, wife of Shivji, also drank of this nectar of devotional love and was filled with joy. In Shri Krishna's loving devotion, the entire company of the cowherds, cowherd-women, and cowherd children of Vraj drank this nectar of love and became overwhelmed with divine feeling.

(This was heard as a saying about the Word from the mouth of Bhagat Gokulbhai Dwarkadas, a poet, of Kudeda.)

_Vachan pakade so mard hai, maheri sab sansaar |_
_Pandya to randya bhaya, bhetya nahi bharathaar ||7||_

(He who firmly grasps the Word alone is truly brave; to him the whole world is like his own obedient wife. The scholars and pandits, by contrast, have become like wandering women who have never met their true husband.)

_Vachanna mahelmein vachan diya kare, ved katebathi vaat nyaari |_
_Brahmka mahalmein brahm bhadka kare, guruna naam par jaay vaari ||8||_

(In the palace of the Word, the Word alone bestows the Word — a matter altogether different from what the Vedas and the Quran declare. In the palace of Brahm-knowledge, Brahm flares up as a mere flash; I offer myself in sacrifice to the Guru's name alone.)

_Vachan aar hai vachan paar hai, vachan gam gheriyo |_
_Vachanse vachan neepaje, vohi sadguru ki deriyo ||9||_

(The Word is the support, the Word is the final goal; hold fast to the path, the understanding, of the Word. From the Word the true Word is born — and that alone is the dwelling place of the Sadguru.)

Meaning: he who recognises the Word is truly courageous and wise; for him, the world — maya — becomes obedient to him like a wife under his command. Pandits and scholars, by contrast, wander about like unfaithful women who have never truly met their rightful husband. In the domain of the Word, the words of the Guru and the saints act like a guiding lamp, dispelling ignorance through their teaching. The words they utter are unlike anything found in the Vedas or the Quran. In the atmosphere of Brahm-knowledge and philosophical learning, mere philosophy gives only a flicker of light before going out — flashing on and off like an inconstant devotee's resolve. But when the Guru's own instructive words are uttered, then even the flare of Brahm-knowledge is offered up in sacrifice before them; one abandons the mere flickering talk of Brahm-knowledge and surrenders oneself entirely to the Guru. Thus the Word is "aar" — that is, it has firm support — and the Word is "paar" — that is, it carries final, decisive certainty. One should hold fast to, that is, keep firmly encircled, the path of such a Word. Only from such words will the true Word be born, and that Word alone is the true dwelling place of the Sadguru.

Bhagat Trikambhai Gordhanbhai of Suyadhoda, in his diary of the year 1978, on page 193, has written the following concerning the Word:

1. The Word itself is God (Samagam).
2. For the sake of the Word, the Pandavas surrendered their kingdom and Draupadi to the Kauravas (Mahabharat).
4. For the sake of the Word, King Nal endured exile in the forest (Nalakhyan).
5. For the sake of the Word, King Harishchandra sold his own wife and son (Mahabharat).
6. For the sake of the Word, Lord Vaman became a doorkeeper in the house of King Bali (Mahabharat).
7. For the sake of the Word, Dhruv, at his stepmother's word, went into the forest and endured great hardship (Mahabharat).
8. For the sake of the Word, Sudhanva entered a cauldron of boiling oil.
9. For the sake of the Word, the descendants of Pratap Rana keep straw as their bed, in fulfilment of their vow (History).
10. For the sake of the Word, the Sikh people wear the bangle (kangan), the vermilion mark (kanku), and the comb (kaanchko).
11. For the sake of the Word, Edward the Eighth gave up the throne of Britain.
12. For the sake of the Word, Pratap Rao Gaekwad too gave up the throne of Vadodara.
13. For the sake of the Word, Narsinh Mehta left his home at his sister-in-law's word.
13/1. For the sake of the Word, Tulsidas left the household life at Ratnavali's word.
14. For the sake of the Word, Vitthaldas Maharaj, descendant of Jivanji Maharaj of Puniyad, stood holding a horse through an entire night.
15. For the sake of the Word, Jadunath gave up eating in company and lived until his final moment on fruit alone.

A chhappo (six-line verse):

He who did not keep his word lost the fruit of all his good deeds. He who did not keep his word died an unnatural death. He who did not keep his word was punished by God Himself. He who did not keep his word had his head and body marked with shame (mundan, the shaving of the head). Whoever became unfaithful to his word lost all his divine splendour (daivat = the oil of divine glory). Shamal says: he who does not keep his word — once the word is gone, what is left at all?

In the ledger of the Shasak Printing Press are further examples of keeping one's word:

1. For the sake of serving the saints, Ghana Bhagat fed the saints his entire stock of wheat-grain.
2. For the sake of serving the saints, Kelaiya offered up his own life as sacrifice.
3. For the sake of serving the saints, Baba Kabir dared to commit theft.
4. For the sake of serving the saints, Pipa Bhagat and Sita Mata pawned their own clothes.
5. Dama Bhagat used up all his grain, and Lord Damodar came to his aid.
6. King Shibi offered up the flesh of his own body for the protection of a refugee.

Even in this Kali Yuga, in an age piled high with deceit and treachery, such kings and rulers too have shown courage in keeping the rule of righteous conduct. Let us understand Kabirji's words further.

_Kahet kabir ram ras paayo, peevanhaar na paau re ||_

(Kabir says: I have obtained the nectar of Ram, yet I find no one to drink it with me.)

That is, the Guru has given Kabirji the nectar of Ram; this nectar is such that only once one has drunk it can one savour its true delight — but those who cannot recognise it, whose minds remain fixed on sensory objects and their disturbances, cannot recognise this nectar nor enjoy its delight. That is why Kabirji says: I myself have drunk it, and I offer it to others too, but even when I offer it, whoever does not drink it — how can I make him drink? Such wretched souls simply cannot understand it. Yet the further question arises: how, then, is this to be recognised? How is one to believe that this is indeed the Guru's word? Only through practice (abhyas) — that is, through sustained effort — should one strive to understand it. And it must be understood through the impressions (sanskaras) carried over from past lives. Moreover, we should come to know this word "Ram" by following those who, before us, have already known it. Jivanji Maharaj says—

_Ramanande je kahi, so suni das kabir |_
_So sadguru kahi jivana, bhaj sitapati raghuvir ||10||_

(What Ramanand spoke, that was heard by Das Kabir; and that same word the Sadguru speaks, O Jivana — worship the Lord of Sita, the hero of the Raghu line.)

That is, this Guru-word has come down even from before Jivanji Maharaj himself; it is this very word that Jivanji Maharaj has received and shown to us. Further—

_Sadgurukhe updeshka, aradh naam pravesh |_
_Bhavsagar mitke jivana, hum aavenge unadesh ||11||_

(Through the Sadguru's teaching, entry may be gained even through half the Name; and through it, O Jivana, once the ocean of worldly existence is crossed away, we shall arrive at that far shore.)

Meaning: through the name "Ram," which the Sadguru has given, if one grasps and practises even half that word — that is, the syllable "Ra" alone — with faith, that alone gives the power to cross the ocean of worldly existence and reach that far shore.

Jivanji Maharaj says: for this, we must now make the effort — for—

_Aagha mata saadhka, jahaan parbrahmaki aas |_
_Poora mata tahaan jivana, jahaan sadguru shabd vishwas ||12||_

(The seeker's understanding is but partial where there is only longing for Parbrahm; the understanding is complete, O Jivana, only where there is faith in the Sadguru's word.)

Meaning: even if one grasps, with faith, only half of the divine Name "Ram" given by the Sadguru — that is, the syllable "Ra" alone — one can still cross the ocean of worldly existence. But should someone, without ever having received the name Ram or any other divine name from the Sadguru, believe that by the divine name alone he can cross this ocean, or that through japa, austerity, vows and the like he may attain heaven and such, and so set the Guru aside and worship in his own self-willed manner — then, for such a devotee, whatever devotion he practises through the divine name, his understanding remains only half true. But one who, having received the divine name from the Sadguru, practises devotion with faith placed in it, attains the complete and entire fulfilment of God. Whereas without the Sadguru, one attains only an incomplete fulfilment of God. For—

_Aadha mata kaun kaamka, je paave vaikunthko dhaam |_
_Taathe jagat bhali jivana, kabahu sant sangat vishraam ||13||_
(Sant)

(Of what use is a half-true understanding, even if it should attain the abode of Vaikunth? Better than that, O Jivana, is this world itself, where at times one may find rest and repose in the company of saints.)

Meaning: whatever fruit is gained through the performance of ordinary religious duties, or through japa, austerity, vows, sacrifices, and the like — of what use is that, when it leads merely to Vaikunth or heaven? Far better than attaining such a place is to take birth in this very world — for at least, at times, in this world one gets the chance to dwell in the company of saints, an opportunity that is not possible in Vaikunth or the like.

The seeker can traverse half the road, for his yearning, his longing to attain Parbrahm, has reached its highest pitch of intensity; by the sheer force of that yearning he has already completed half the journey. But the remaining road must be travelled onward through practice, placing faith in the Sadguru's word.

_Pakh chhooti dohodish gai, rahyo sant samagam saar |_
_Sadguru shabde jivana, utariye peli paar ||14||_

(All partisan leanings, in every direction, have fallen away; what remains, as the very essence, is the company of saints. By the Sadguru's word, O Jivana, we shall cross over to that far shore.)

Meaning: there was once a clash of sects and differing doctrines, a confusion over which path — japa, austerity, vows, sacrifice, pilgrimage, and the other paths of religious duty — one ought to follow. From this confusion the seeker has now become free, and, from every direction, from every side, he has resolved to hold fast to one single support alone, and through that support to make the essence of all essences the company of saints (sant samagam). By walking in accordance with the Sadguru's teaching, one shall be able to cross to the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence.

The obstruction of factional leanings has now fallen away, because one has taken hold of the Sadguru's hand — hence every obstruction shall be removed, and the bondage of sectarian directions too has been removed. Only the essential words that come through the company of saints now remain, and by means of these one shall reach the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence with ease.

_Jahaan sadgurukaa dava nahi, tahaan jamka dava hoy |_
_Raam bharunse jivana, bharam pado mat koi ||15||_

(Where there is no claim of the Sadguru, there Death's claim holds sway; trust in Ram alone, O Jivana — let none fall into delusion.)

_Hari bhaje hari na paaiye, sab aap aapkun dhaay |_
_Guru samasa bin jivana, kaal jhapete jaay ||16||_

(One may worship Hari and still not attain Hari, for each runs merely after his own self-interest; without the Guru's true direction, O Jivana, one is snatched away by the grip of Death.)

Knowledge without a Guru is like an incomplete education, and the finest example of this is given by the story of Narad Muni in the Puranas. That is why Jivanji Maharaj explains: however learned a person may be, without the recognition of the Sadguru he remains unhappy and suffers. Whatever direction — whatever hint or gesture — the Guru points toward, if one fails to grasp it, one falls into the grip of death. Only through the Guru's words can one become gurumukh, for—

_Sadguru sabad bin jivana, jyun andho aarasi paay ||17||_

(Without the Sadguru's word, O Jivana, it is as if a blind man were handed a mirror.)

If a mirror is placed before a blind man, it is of no use whatsoever, for he cannot even see his own face in it. Kabirji, describing the glory of the Guru, likewise says that through the Guru's influence his own speech has been utterly transformed — what was once bitter has become sweet.

_Kabir vaani hamaari palti, ya mulak ya desh |_
_Khaari te meethi bhai, sadgurukhe updesh ||18||_

(Kabir says: my speech has been utterly transformed — in this land, in this country — that which was bitter has become sweet, through the teaching of the Sadguru.)

For Kabirji also says, reflecting on the Sadguru's word—

_Kabir shabd vichaari jo chale, guru mukh hoye nihaal |_
_Kaam krodh vyaape nahi, kabahu na graase kaal ||19||_

(Kabir says: whoever walks having reflected on the Word becomes gurumukh and is made joyful and fulfilled; lust and anger no longer take hold of him, and Death can never seize him.)

Without the Guru, the true path cannot be attained. This subject will be discussed further ahead in greater detail. Looking further here, Jivanji Maharaj says that, as Jaidevji's words spoken earlier had it — patati patatre — "when a leaf falls, when a leaf stirs" — for the joy of union, Lord Krishna once went to the appointed forest bower, and there, restless with longing for Radhaji's arrival, believed that at even the stirring of a single leaf Radhaji must be arriving, and so, filled with eager anticipation, began preparing a welcome for her. In just this way, should any devotee show even the slightest willingness to act according to the gurumukh's word and teaching, then just as the Lord holds such eagerness to welcome Radha, He holds the very same eagerness to meet such a devotee. While Jaidev's Geet Govind was being sung, the Lord followed after the daughter of a garland-maker who was gathering flowers — for such is the glory of these paramount words: they are themselves the very form of God made manifest. In the Adi Purana there is a verse.

_Madbhaktaa yatra gacchanti tatra gacchaami paarthiva |_
_Bhaktaanaamanugacchanti muktayah shrutibhih saha ||8||_

(O Partha, wherever My devotees go, there I go too; and liberation itself, together with the Vedas, follows after such devotees.)

Meaning: O Partha, wherever My devotees go, there I go too; and liberation too, together with the Vedas, follows after such devotees. Here, seeing the disposition (bhava) of King Ambarish, Krishna had withdrawn from sight and had to come back again — for when there is faith in the Guru's word, Kripanath must come. That is why we say the Word itself is the Supreme, and Kabirji, too, confirms this through the bhajan quoted above — as when he says, I have obtained the nectar of Ram, yet find none to drink it with me — I long to give it, yet why can I find no one to drink it? And if I do find someone, why do they still not drink?

This is indeed a difficult, knotty question — that the nectar of Ram is to be given, yet none is ready to drink it — how is this to be understood, and what does it mean? Kabirji explains: I have offered the taste of this nectar to many, yet some unwise people cannot understand its true savour — what, then, is to be said to such wretched souls? And further, some, though wise, cannot bring themselves to practise it — for them too, where is one to go even to shed tears? Kabirji says that for such people it is entirely useless even to speak of dharma, for—

_Is loknakun bahe jaan de — hansa, is loknakun bahe jaan de |_
_Hansa hans mili chalo re sarovar, bagahikun medak khaan de ||1||_

(Let these people go their own way, O swan — let these people go their own way. Come, O swan, let us go together to the lake; leave the frogs to be eaten by the herons.)

That is, those who, knowing full well, wish only to fall into the pit — how can such people be stopped? That is why Kabirji says: should you meet a true seeker of saintly company, give him to drink the elixir of Ram; but should you fall among the worldly-minded, they will only caw and croak like crows — words that carry no meaning at all. Wise souls, then, should not waste their time on such people but should press onward themselves — for the path of saints is one thing entirely, while the path of the worldly-minded is filled with quarrel and strife, and further, is steeped in maya, delusion, and attachment. The wise should abandon such company and themselves consider the path by which Parbrahm may be attained through devotion. Kabir says—

(Raga Godi)

_Hari ras saar santo, raam ras saar, je re peeve taako mite re vikaara ||Teka||_
_Hari ras amal saval sun bhaai, amaldaar koi peevega |_
_Je re peeve so hoy avinaasi, amar jugojug jeevega ||1||_
_E ras sanakaadik piya, or umiyaapati swaami |_
_Naaradse muni ketiek varanu, jogeshwar nij naami ||2||_
_Ya sun sharan tumhaare aayo, sitaapati raghunaatha |_
_Daas kabir aharnish peeve, hari ras santo saatha ||3||_

(O saints, the nectar of Hari, the nectar of Ram, is the very essence — whoever drinks it, all his disorders of desire are removed. Listen, brothers, to the true intoxication of Hari's nectar: only a true intoxicant will drink of it; whoever drinks it becomes imperishable, and lives on, immortal, through age after age. This nectar was drunk by the Sanakadik sages and by Umiyapati Shiva, the Lord Himself. How many renowned yogis, beginning with Narad, could I even name? Hearing of this, O Lord of Sita, Raghunath, I have come to Your refuge; Your servant Kabir drinks this nectar of Hari day and night, together with the saints.)

Meaning: O saints, the nectar of Hari alone is the highest essence; whoever drinks it, his disorders of desire are removed. Let me tell you of the effect of the intoxication that this nectar of Hari brings — listen: only one who is a true intoxicant will drink of it and savour its taste. Whoever drinks it becomes imperishable, indestructible, and lives on through age upon age. This nectar has been drunk by the Sanakadik sages and by Umapati Mahadev; how many could one even count among Narad and the other renowned yogis? Hearing the praises of this nectar, O Sitapati Ram, I have come to Your refuge. Your servant Kabir drinks this nectar day and night, together with the saints.

_Samajhe naraku hari kathaa, ana samajhekun haaji |_
_Sabad sabad aanti pade, jaise doodhmein kaanji ||20||_

(To the one who understands, the story of Hari is received as understanding; to the one who does not understand, only mindless agreement follows. Word tangles against word, as when vinegar is dropped into milk.)

Meaning: if something is told to a wise person, he receives the discourse on God with the love with which he would listen to it; but the unwise person, without understanding, simply keeps saying "yes, yes" — and further, whatever we say to him, he twists every word we speak and takes offence, just as milk curdles and splits when vinegar falls into it, so too does such an unwise person turn against us in resentment.

The name of this Ram-elixir should be given only where there is one who can understand it as it truly is — for only where there is one able to understand the name "Ram" should the "Name" be used at all. However precious a diamond may be, if the jeweller's power of discernment is weak, he cannot rightly appraise its true worth. So too, only before one who is a true connoisseur of the real diamond should the matter of the Ram-elixir be spoken — only then can its true worth be understood. If no one capable of recognising it is found, it will be treated with contempt. Thus, since the Guru's word is precious, it must be spread and propagated only in such a way that its importance is preserved — and it should never be given to anyone unworthy; that is, the name "Ram" should not even be uttered in front of them.

In society, there are many who never utter the name "Ramkabir." If one greets them first with the name "Ramkabir," they simply stand with folded hands in silence, or else, instead of "Ramkabir," they will utter the name of whatever other path or sect they are affiliated with or influenced by. Before such people the name "Ramkabir" should not be uttered, nor should they be urged to utter it — for neither side gains any benefit from it. For Jivanji Maharaj, through the words of Narsinh Mehta, says—

_Jire dhanyatun dhanyatun em kahe shri hari, narasaiya tun maaro bhakt saacho |_
_Meli purushaatan, sakhi re veshe thayo, taahera premthi hun re naachyo ||_
_Jire mujmaan tujmaan, bhed nahi naagaraa, maan tun maahyari ved vaani |_
_Haju tane pratit na upaje, me tane mokalyun taadhun paani |_
_Mosaalu kidhun te kem gayo visari, haar aapyo pratyaksh bhoop |_
_Chaud lokmaan mahaare tuj samo ko nahi, taaharu maaharu ek roop |_
_Taahara akshar gaayane saambhle, tehnaa kuntumb sahit paavan thaaye |_
_Bhane narasaiyo meethaan boli su rijavo, taare kar jodi krishnaji sam khaaye ||_

(Blessed, blessed indeed — thus Shri Hari says — Narsinh, you are My true devotee; you laid aside your manhood and took the guise of a sakhi, and I danced for love of you. There is no difference at all, O Nagar, between you and Me; accept this as My own true, Veda-like word. If you still do not believe it — I sent you cool water in your hour of need; I performed your mother-in-law's ritual gift for you — how could you have forgotten that? I gave you, in person, a garland with My own hand. In all the fourteen worlds there is none like you; yours and Mine are, in truth, a single form. Whoever hears your verses sung is purified, together with his whole family. Narsinh says: pleased by such sweet words, I fold my hands, and Krishnaji Himself swears an oath to it.)

"Blessed, blessed are you" — that is, here, beyond all identification with the body, an unbroken identity (tadatmya) has been forged between the jiva and Parbrahm — a bond not made through the outer senses. Free of the false distinction that says "this is the body, this is the soul," this is a non-dual oneness, free of every disorder belonging to the objects of the senses — a pure, conscious identity with Parbrahm. This is the very "Ram-rasa" of which Kabirji has spoken; and the drinker of that nectar he spoke of is none other than the devotee Narsinh Mehta, who has drunk of this Ram-rasa. Having tasted that nectar, he became wholly "Ram-formed" (Rammaya). Every kind of distinction and bondage has fallen away from him, for now there is no difference left at all between the man of Nagar, Narsaiya, and Parbrahm. Men are not granted entry into Lord Krishna's Ras. Narsinh Mehta abandoned his identity as a man and, showing the disposition of a woman, drank of the nectar of the Ras. Such is the state of one who becomes wholly immersed in the nectar of Hari's love — and in his pad on spring, Narsinh Mehta says:

_Je harine ojhalade aave, te purush panun vege visare |_

(Whoever comes into the very shadow of Hari's presence swiftly forgets his own manhood.)

Meaning: whoever comes within the shadow of Hari's loving devotion swiftly forgets his own manhood, his masculine identity. (Udadharma Panchratnamala, page 426, 4th edition.)

Such is the effect of the taste of divine love upon whoever drinks of that nectar of love, and this same effect befell Narsinh Mehta. Sundardas has sung of this in a savaiya:

_Jo man naariki or nihaarat, to man hot naarike roopaa |_
_Jo man kaahusu krodh bicharat, to man hai bahi tad roopaa ||1||_
_Jo man maayaa hi maayaa rate, to man padat hai maayake koopa |_
_Sundar jo man brahm bicharat, to man hot hai brahmamay tadroopaa ||2||_

(If the mind gazes toward a woman, the mind itself takes on the form of a woman. If the mind dwells in anger against someone, the mind itself flows into that very form of anger. If the mind only ever chants maya, maya, the mind falls into the very well of maya. Sundar says: if the mind contemplates Brahm, the mind itself becomes Brahm-formed, of that very same nature.)

Meaning: if the mind dwells on thoughts of a woman, the mind itself takes on the form of a woman; and if the mind dwells on anger toward someone, the mind itself becomes anger-formed. If the mind only chants "maya, maya," the mind falls into the very well of maya. Sundardas says: if the mind contemplates Brahm-Parbrahm, the mind itself becomes wholly Brahm-Parbrahm-formed.

In the Harmala it is said, "I drink in the whole of the crores of universes." In the pad of supplication it is said:

_Maahaare jahevi vraj sundari tehvo jan narasaiyo |_
_Ine niramal mane maaharo jas gaao |_
_Jire tunj leelaae madhukar kunj maadhavaa |_
_Purush naame koi paas na aave |_

(Narsaiya, this devotee, is to Me just like the beautiful women of Vraj; with a pure mind he has sung My glory. In Your bower-play, O Madhava, roaming like a bee, no one bearing the name of manhood may draw near.)

Meaning: Krishna says: for Me, this Narsinh Mehta is just like the beautiful women of Vraj. With a pure mind he has sung My praises. In the play of the bower in Vrindavan, where Krishna roamed like a bee, drinking the love-nectar of the cowherd-women, no one bearing the mark of manhood can even approach this play. Thus Narsinh Mehta too, setting aside his own manhood, drank of the nectar of the Ras-lila in the disposition of a gopi — for the Narad Bhakti Sutra says—

_Tanmayah_

(Becoming wholly absorbed, one with Him.)

That is, to become wholly absorbed and one with Him — the devotee becomes so immersed in God that he forgets his own separate form. Here no distinction remains at all. Shandilya Muni says—

_Ananya bhaktyaa tad buddhi bundaatyalayaantam |_

(Through single-minded, undivided devotion, the discriminating intellect dissolves entirely into That.)

Through undivided devotion, once that discriminating intellect (bheda-buddhi) is fully dissolved, the oneness of atma and Parbrahm is accomplished.

_Kabir main jaanu hari door hai, hari rahyaa sakal bharapoor |_
_Aap pechhaanaa baaheraa, teraa hi te door ||21||_

(Kabir says: I once thought Hari was far away, yet Hari is present, filling all things entirely. It is your own self that has strayed outward — it is that very straying that has kept you far from Him.)

_Kabir meraa saain mujhmein, bhamyo naanaa ne taas |_
_Kasturi kaa mrig jyaun, phir phir sudhe dhaas ||22||_

(Kabir says: my Lord is within me, yet I wandered about in every direction searching for Him — like the musk-deer who runs here and there, again and again, chasing after the scent of grass.)

_Kabir ja karan jag dhundhiya, so to ghatahi maanhi |_
_Pardaa diyaa bharmakaa, taaten soojhe naahi ||23||_

(Kabir says: that which he searched for throughout the world was, all along, within his own body — but a veil of delusion had been drawn, and so it could not be seen.)

_Kabir ham jaanaa hari door hai, lok vedki chhaanhi |_
_Giri gehvar dhoondhat phire, hari biraaje ghatmaanhi ||24||_

(Kabir says: we thought Hari was far away, under the shade of worldly custom and scripture; we wandered searching through mountains and caves, while Hari all along dwelt within our own being.)

_Kabir daudat daudat daudiyaa, jab lagi manki daud |_
_Daud thaki man thir bhaayaa, vast thaurki thaur ||25||_

(Kabir says: I ran and ran and kept on running, for as long as the mind's own restless running lasted; when the running wearied and the mind at last grew still, the sought-for thing was found right there, in its own place.)

That is: if, without understanding the Sadguru's word, one keeps running here and there like the musk-deer chasing after fragrance and flavour, one will only end up exhausted and, in the end, must come right back to where one began. One should not go wandering about anywhere in search of Parbrahm; rather, one should place faith in the Sadguru and live one's life accordingly. Jivanji Maharaj has truly taught the Udabhakta community how to live a true life — but how, then, should one live? We shall look at the answer to this question further ahead. There Jivandasji spoke — what did he speak?
